gaps: No source directly compares live multi-small-model orchestration against single-model distillation of multi-agent behavior on the same task set (the specific ProST-vs-MapCoder-Lite-style comparison flagged as opportunistic step 5) -- 'Can Small Agents Collaborate to Beat a Single Large Language Model?' (2601.11327) shows live small-agent orchestration beating a single larger model, but not against a distilled single small model, so the direct comparison remains unfound.

Counter-evidence on fine-tuning/distillation for agentic/coding capability (opportunistic step 5, second half) surfaced only tangentially: two independent sources (Phantom Transfer 2607.10750, Unintended Misalignment 2508.14031) show fine-tuning-induced safety/misalignment risk, not a capability-ceiling limitation, and neither tests small (sub-10B) models specifically (both use 70B-class or unspecified-size models).

Several architectural/context-management sources (ATOD 2606.27814, CacheRL 2606.14179, Beyond Compaction 2606.11213) were identified and characterized only from search-engine summaries, not independently fetched and read in full -- flagged in sources.json as lower-confidence, partial-coverage entries pending direct verification if a future round is warranted.

AgenticQwen (2604.21590) makes a strong 'closes the gap with much larger models' claim but its specific numeric benchmark comparisons were not extractable from the fetched content -- the claim is recorded as directional/unverified rather than quantified.

The single strongest ceiling-raising-looking result (SCoRe / 2509.14257, a 7B student exceeding a 72B teacher on 12 agentic benchmarks) has directional corroboration from the same technique cluster (AgenticQwen, ATOD, CacheRL) but no source independently re-executed or replicated SCoRe's own benchmark numbers -- per the plan's explicit skepticism requirement, this should be treated as a single-source claim pending independent replication, not an established fact.
summary: One gathering round produced 19 sources directly responsive to the plan's five research steps. Coverage: (1) architectural/system-level techniques for small models -- context management (ACM), memory systems (LightMem), execution feedback (Feedback Over Form), self-compaction (SelfCompact), and RL-training stabilization (Towards Robust RL for Small-Scale Agents) -- with the standout finding being ACM's own negative admission that sub-9B models were too incoherent to even train their context-management technique on, a data point for a possible scale floor. (2) Recent work with multi-turn/long-horizon collapse as its primary subject (HORIZON/Long-Horizon Task Mirage, OdysseyArena), though both test only frontier-scale models, not small ones -- relevance to small models is inferred and flagged as such. (3) Direct evidence on both sides of the fundamental-limit-vs-solvable-gap question: 'On the Fundamental Limits of LLMs at Scale' argues for intrinsic theoretical barriers (general-LLM framing, not small-model-specific); 'Towards Reasoning Ability of Small Language Models' (ThinkSLM) argues training/data quality matters more than scale across 72 SLMs; HORIZON explicitly argues scaling alone won't resolve long-horizon failure. (4) A cluster of structurally-distinct-within-distillation techniques (SCoRe, AgenticQwen, ATOD, CacheRL) all targeting multi-turn agentic gap-closing specifically, headlined by SCoRe's strong single-source claim of a 7B student exceeding a 72B teacher, deliberately flagged per the plan's own skepticism mandate as unreplicated. (5) Opportunistic: live orchestration evidence (Can Small Agents Collaborate, Beyond the Strongest LLM) and fine-tuning/distillation counter-evidence (two independent misalignment-risk papers) were found but only partially answer the two flagged secondary questions, as detailed in gaps above.
